method: One researcher per topic (official sources only) followed by an independent fact-checker per topic. Evidence tiers are recorded per claim.

claims.statement: The comment resource identifies its author with snippet.authorDisplayName, snippet.authorProfileImageUrl, snippet.authorChannelUrl and snippet.authorChannelId.value; only authorChannelId.value is defined as the author's YouTube channel ID, and the authorChannelId object is documented as present only 'if any' (it can be absent).
claims.quote: Contains the id of the author's YouTube channel, if any.
claims.design_implication: Match comments to members only by exact equality on snippet.authorChannelId.value, and treat a comment with no authorChannelId as unattributable (unverified).

claims.statement: Google's 'Implementation: Comments' guide itself decides authorship by comparing a comment's snippet.authorChannelId.value with the authenticated user's channel ID; authorDisplayName is described only as 'The name of the user who posted the comment' and no official text seen calls it unique or immutable. (Guide wording seen only via search summary; display-name description read in the discovery document.)
claims.design_implication: Channel-ID equality is the documented attribution test, so it can back a 'verified' label, while a display-name, avatar or URL-text match can never be more than 'unverified' or 'manually reviewed'.

claims.statement: The signed-in member's channel ID is obtained with channels.list and mine=true, which returns the channels owned by the authenticated user (the 'Work with Channel IDs' guide gives channels.list(part="id", mine=true), per search summary); because it depends on the authenticated user it requires an OAuth token and cannot be done with an API key alone.
claims.quote: Return the ids of channels owned by the authenticated user.
claims.design_implication: A member's channel ID may only be treated as platform-attested when it comes from that member's own OAuth-authorized channels.list?mine=true response, not from a typed-in handle or URL.

claims.statement: channels.list accepts five OAuth scopes (youtube, youtube.force-ssl, youtube.readonly, youtubepartner, youtubepartner-channel-audit); youtube.readonly, described as 'View your YouTube account', is the narrowest read-only one, so it is the minimum scope for the mine=true lookup ('minimum' is a reading of the scope list, not a sentence in the docs).
claims.design_implication: Request only youtube.readonly at sign-in and use that token for nothing except the channel-ID lookup.

claims.statement: The docs seen do not define what mine=true returns for an account with no channel or with several channels: the response is described only as zero or more channel resources; the errors page documents 401 youtubeSignupRequired for an 'unlinked' Google Account that has no YouTube channel; YouTube Help says one Google Account can manage many Brand Account channels (up to 100) and that some third-party tools using API authentication do not support channel switching and fall back to a default channel.
claims.design_implication: Handle empty items and youtubeSignupRequired as 'no channel linked, cannot verify', and show the returned channel to the member for confirmation instead of assuming it is the channel they comment from.

claims.statement: Neither commentThreads.list nor comments.list can filter by author channel: commentThreads.list accepts only part, allThreadsRelatedToChannelId, channelId, id, videoId, maxResults, moderationStatus, order, pageToken, searchTerms and textFormat; comments.list accepts only part, id, parentId, maxResults, pageToken and textFormat. The one content filter, searchTerms, matches key words, not authors, and cannot be combined with the id filter.
claims.quote: Limits the returned comment threads to those matching the specified key words. Not compatible with the 'id' filter.
claims.design_implication: To show that channel X commented on video V the app must page commentThreads.list?videoId=V (optionally narrowed by searchTerms on text the member supplies) and compare authorChannelId.value itself; an incomplete scan must be reported as 'not checked fully', never as 'did not comment'.

claims.statement: The replies part of a commentThread contains only 'a limited number of replies' (no number is documented) and is complete only when its count equals snippet.totalReplyCount; the full reply list is retrieved with comments.list using parentId set to the top-level comment ID (the commentThreads reference says to use comments.list with parentId, per search summary).
claims.quote: A limited number of replies. Unless the number of replies returned equals total_reply_count in the snippet the returned replies are only a subset of the total number of replies.
claims.design_implication: Reply-type activity can only be confirmed by an extra comments.list?parentId= call for every thread whose embedded replies are fewer than totalReplyCount.

claims.statement: comments.list has no videoId parameter: its parentId parameter returns replies to one specified comment, and YouTube is documented as having only one level of replies (replies to top-level comments), with a note that replies to replies may be supported in the future.
claims.quote: Returns replies to the specified comment. Note, currently YouTube features only one level of replies (ie replies to top level comments).
claims.design_implication: Finding a member's reply requires first enumerating the video's threads and then expanding each thread, so reply verification costs at least one extra call per expanded thread.

claims.statement: The API overview and authorization guide state the general rule that every request must carry either an API key or an OAuth 2.0 token, that API keys are for public data, and that OAuth is required for private user data and for insert/update/delete; reading published comments of a public video with an API key alone follows from that rule, but the comment reference pages were not seen stating it explicitly.
claims.design_implication: Read comments server-side with the project's API key so that verification never depends on, or exposes, a member's token.

claims.statement: When commentThreads.list or comments.list is called with OAuth instead of an API key, the only scope listed for both methods is youtube.force-ssl, which grants 'See, edit, and permanently delete your YouTube videos, ratings, comments and captions'; youtube.readonly is not listed for these two methods.
claims.quote: See, edit, and permanently delete your YouTube videos, ratings, comments and captions
claims.design_implication: Do not read comments with a member's OAuth token, because that would require asking three members for a write-and-delete scope the dashboard has no need for.

claims.statement: Documented errors (per search summaries): commentThreads.list returns 403 commentsDisabled when the video identified by videoId has disabled comments, 404 videoNotFound, 404 channelNotFound, 400 processingFailure and 400 operationNotSupported; comments.list returns 400 operationNotSupported, 403 forbidden (insufficient permissions or not properly authorized) and 404 commentNotFound. The errors index also lists 403 forbidden and 404 commentThreadNotFound for commentThreads.list, and the summaries disagree on whether the method page lists those two.
claims.design_implication: Map each error to its own non-verified state (comments disabled, video not found, not permitted, retry later) and never collapse an error into 'member did not comment'.

claims.statement: commentThreads.list moderationStatus defaults to published (discovery document: default 'published', 'The comment is available for public display.'), so a normal listing returns only publicly displayed comments; per search summaries of the reference pages, the parameter 'can only be used in a properly authorized request' to fetch heldForReview or likelySpam threads, and snippet.moderationStatus is returned only when the request is authorized by the owner of the channel or video the comments are on.
claims.design_implication: A member's comment that is held for review or flagged as likely spam is invisible to this app, so 'not found' must be worded as 'no public comment found', not as proof that nothing was posted.

claims.statement: The docs describe no tombstone or 'deleted' state for comments: a video with comments disabled produces 403 commentsDisabled rather than an empty list, and a comment that is later deleted, rejected or held simply stops appearing in the default published listing (a lookup by ID is documented to return 404 commentNotFound when a comment cannot be found). The app cannot distinguish deleted from hidden from never-posted.
claims.design_implication: Record a verification as a dated observation (comment ID, publishedAt, time checked) and on later disappearance show 'no longer publicly visible' instead of asserting deletion or silently keeping a live 'verified' badge.

claims.statement: The official API description does not address Shorts for comments: the only occurrence of 'Shorts' in the v3 discovery document (revision 20261106) is an image aspect-ratio description, commentThreads.list takes a generic videoId, and search of the reference pages found Shorts mentioned only for viewCount semantics. That Shorts use the same video IDs and the same comment endpoints as regular videos is therefore inferred, not stated.
claims.quote: Returns the comment threads of the specified video.
claims.design_implication: Route Shorts through the same code path but confirm with a real request against a known Short before labelling Shorts comment activity 'verified'.

claims.statement: Default quota, per search summaries of the overview page and revision history: 10,000 units per day combined for all endpoints other than search.list and videos.insert, which since a June 1, 2026 'granular quota' change each have their own bucket of 100 calls per day; daily quota resets at midnight Pacific Time and the default is stated to be subject to change.
claims.design_implication: All comment, channel and video reads share one 10,000-unit daily bucket, so the app should avoid search.list entirely and budget thread scans against that bucket.

claims.statement: Per search summaries of the Quota Calculator and method pages, commentThreads.list, comments.list, channels.list and videos.list each cost 1 quota unit per call (each page is a call), every request including an invalid one costs at least one unit, and an exhausted quota returns HTTP 403 with reason quotaExceeded.
claims.design_implication: On quotaExceeded the app must stop and show 'check not completed, will retry after quota reset' rather than downgrading or upgrading any label.

claims.statement: maxResults limits read from the discovery document: commentThreads.list 1-100 (default 20), comments.list 1-100 (default 20), channels.list 0-50 (default 5), videos.list 1-50 (default 5, and not supported together with the id parameter).
claims.quote: The *maxResults* parameter specifies the maximum number of items that should be returned in the result set.
claims.design_implication: A full scan of a video with T top-level threads costs about ceil(T/100) units plus at least one unit per expanded reply thread, so scans of very large videos need a cap and an explicit 'scan incomplete' outcome.

claims.statement: Revision-history entries for 2025-2026 reported by search summaries: September 30, 2026 added snippet.imageUrl to the comments resource (the property is confirmed in the discovery document as a signed link that expires six hours after retrieval); March 31, 2025 changed Shorts view counting in videos/channels statistics.viewCount; an August 2026 entry (summaries give both August 24 and August 27) redefines viewCount to count a view when playback begins. No surfaced entry changes the author fields or the list parameters of comments, commentThreads or channels.
claims.design_implication: Attribution logic is unaffected, but imageUrl values must not be stored, image-only comments must be tolerated, and displayed view counts should be labelled 'as reported by YouTube on <date>' because their definition changed in 2025 and 2026.

claims.statement: No method in the YouTube Data API v3 returns the users who liked (or otherwise rated) a given video. The docs do not state this outright; it is inferred from absence: the official API discovery document (revision 20261108) lists exactly eight videos methods (batchGetStats, delete, getRating, insert, list, rate, reportAbuse, update) and, across all 89 methods of all resources, the only rating-read method is videos.getRating, which is scoped to the authorizing user.
claims.quote: Retrieves the ratings that the authorized user gave to a list of specified videos.
claims.design_implication: The app can never show or verify 'who liked video V' from the video side; any like attribution must come from each member's own authorization.

claims.statement: videos.getRating returns, for each requested video ID, the rating given by the user who authorized the request (response items of {videoId, rating}; rating enum in the discovery document is none / like / dislike). The developers.google.com reference page reportedly also lists a fourth value 'unspecified' (search summary only).
claims.quote: Retrieves the ratings that the authorized user gave to a list of specified videos.
claims.design_implication: A 'like' result is an attestation about the consenting account only, and only 'like' (not none/unspecified/error) may map to a verified label.

claims.statement: As of discovery revision 20261108, videos.getRating accepts four OAuth scopes: youtube, youtube.force-ssl, youtube.readonly and youtubepartner (videos.rate, the write method, does not list youtube.readonly).
claims.design_implication: The app can request the read-only scope alone for like checks and never needs a scope that would let it rate, post or manage on the member's behalf.

claims.statement: The YouTube Data API revision history reportedly carries an entry dated September 1, 2026 stating that videos.getRating now accepts the youtube.readonly authorization scope (previously only youtube, youtube.force-ssl and youtubepartner). The date was seen in two independent search summaries, not in the page text; the resulting scope list itself is confirmed verbatim by the discovery document (C3).
claims.design_implication: Older guidance saying a write-capable scope is required for getRating is outdated; design the consent screen around youtube.readonly but confirm the dated entry on the live page.

claims.statement: videos.list with myRating returns only videos liked/disliked by the authenticated (authorizing) user; the method has no parameter for naming another user (its full parameter set is chart, hl, id, locale, maxHeight, maxResults, maxWidth, myRating, onBehalfOfContentOwner, pageToken, part, regionCode, videoCategoryId). Search summaries of the reference page add that myRating can only be used in a properly authorized request and otherwise yields a 403 forbidden error.
claims.quote: Return videos liked/disliked by the authenticated user.
claims.design_implication: A member's liked-video list is readable only with that member's own token; the app cannot audit a non-consenting person's likes.

claims.statement: The liked-videos playlist (channel contentDetails.relatedPlaylists.likes, readable via playlistItems.list) is private to the account owner according to YouTube Help ('only you will be able to see this playlist'), and playlistItems.list documents a 403 playlistItemsNotAccessible error for requests not authorized to retrieve a playlist; so another user's liked playlist is not readable without that user's authorization. The API docs do not spell out which error a third-party request for someone else's likes playlist returns.
claims.design_implication: The playlist route offers no third-party visibility either; it is just a second way to read the consenting member's own likes.

claims.statement: statistics.likeCount, viewCount and commentCount on the video resource are aggregate totals only; the VideoStatistics schema contains just likeCount, dislikeCount, favoriteCount (deprecated), commentCount and viewCount, with no per-user breakdown. The same aggregate-only shape applies to the newer videos.batchGetStats method (up to 50 IDs per call).
claims.quote: The number of users who have indicated that they liked the video by giving it a positive rating.
claims.design_implication: Counts may be displayed as informational statistics but can never support a claim that a specific member contributed to them.

claims.quote: Note that the view count, likes, etc will still be visible if this is disabled.
claims.design_implication: Do not use publicStatsViewable as the signal for whether likeCount will be present; it is unrelated to like-count hiding.

claims.statement: YouTube Help ('Edit video settings', Comments and ratings section) documents a creator setting controlling whether viewers can see a video's like count, but no official API page that could be consulted states whether statistics.likeCount is then omitted from videos.list. The only documented owner-only statistic is dislikeCount (private since December 13, 2021, returned only when the request is authenticated by the video owner). Omission of likeCount when likes are hidden is reported in practice by third-party sources only.
claims.design_implication: Treat likeCount as an optional field and render 'hidden by owner / unavailable' rather than 0 when it is absent.

claims.statement: The Data API revision history reportedly has an August 2026 entry (dated August 27, 2026 in the revision history; the videos and channels reference pages reportedly cite August 24, 2026) saying YouTube aligns public view counting across long-form, Live and Shorts so a public view is counted when a video begins to play; no 2025-2026 entry changing statistics.likeCount was found.
claims.design_implication: viewCount is a platform-defined aggregate whose definition changed in 2026, so label it as YouTube's public view count and avoid comparing pre- and post-change figures as like-for-like.

claims.statement: With a member's own OAuth 2.0 consent the app can check that member's rating of video V by calling videos.getRating with id=V using that member's access token; it requires user authorization (an API key alone is insufficient) under one of the scopes youtube, youtube.force-ssl, youtube.readonly or youtubepartner, and the result reflects the consenting Google account's rating at the moment of the call.
claims.quote: Retrieves the ratings that the authorized user gave to a list of specified videos.
claims.design_implication: 'Verified' is honest only as 'the YouTube account this member connected had rating=like on V when checked at <timestamp>'; it must be re-checked or time-stamped because a like can be removed later.

claims.statement: Google's OAuth documentation says a project whose publishing status is 'Testing' is limited to 100 listed test users and that test-user authorizations (including refresh tokens) expire seven days after consent when the app requests scopes beyond openid/email/profile; public apps requesting sensitive or restricted scopes require Google verification.

claims.statement: YouTube's Fake engagement policy prohibits artificially increasing views, likes, comments or other metrics, and (as relayed by search-index excerpts of the page, not verified against the live page) states that content that solely exists to incentivize viewers for engagement (views, likes, comments, etc) is prohibited, and that engagement is illegitimate when it results from coercion or deception or when its sole purpose is financial gain.
claims.design_implication: The dashboard must not award money, points or prizes in exchange for YouTube likes, comments, views or subscriptions; YouTube numbers should be shown as information only, never as a reward trigger.

claims.statement: The Fake engagement policy explicitly allows simply asking for engagement: search-index excerpts relay a note that creators are allowed to encourage viewers to subscribe, hit the like button, share or leave a comment, while offering to subscribe to another channel only if they subscribe back ('sub4sub') is prohibited.
claims.design_implication: The app may remind members to ask their audience to like or comment, but must not build reciprocal or conditional engagement exchanges between members.

claims.statement: No carve-out permitting rewards in exchange for engagement was found in the Fake engagement or Spam policy excerpts, and the excerpts did not show the words money, points or prizes itemized individually; the prohibition is expressed generically as 'rewards', 'incentivize' and 'financial gain'.
claims.design_implication: Treat any reward type, including internal points, as covered by the generic prohibition rather than assuming non-cash rewards are exempt.

claims.statement: The Spam policy page, as currently indexed, lists 'Engagement manipulation: Repetitive or templated content aimed at artificially inflating engagement through bots, coercion or offering rewards in exchange for likes, views or subscribers', gives coordinated sub-for-sub schemes as an example, and says it is okay to ask viewers to like, comment or subscribe; the heading 'Incentivization Spam' was not found in the indexed text.
claims.design_implication: A points-for-engagement mechanic maps directly onto the 'offering rewards in exchange for likes, views or subscribers' wording and should be excluded from the product.

claims.statement: YouTube permits contests subject to its contest policies: per search-index excerpts the contest must be free of charge to enter, and the organizer and any third party may not manipulate metrics on the YouTube service (views, likes, dislikes or subscribers) to misrepresent genuine viewer engagement.
claims.design_implication: Even a properly run contest cannot use likes, views or subscriber counts as the entry or winning mechanism, so contest status must not be tied to YouTube metrics in the dashboard.

claims.statement: The contest policy requires 'official rules' that link to the YouTube Community Guidelines and disqualify non-compliant entries, state that YouTube is not a sponsor, require entrants to release YouTube from liability, and include a legally compliant privacy notice; the organizer is solely responsible, may not associate YouTube with the contest without prior written consent, may not run it through ad units, and may not require entrants to transfer all rights in their entries.
claims.design_implication: Any contest surfaced in the app needs its own published rules and a YouTube non-sponsorship disclaimer, and the app must never imply YouTube verified or endorsed the contest.

claims.statement: Developer Policies section III.E.4 limits Non-Authorized Data to temporary storage of limited amounts for no longer than 30 calendar days, after which the client must delete or refresh it, and states that statistics retrieved as Non-Authorized Data (for example a channel's subscriber count without the channel owner's authorization) must not be stored for more than 30 days.
claims.design_implication: Public YouTube statistics shown in the dashboard need a stored fetch timestamp and an automatic refresh-or-delete job at 30 days or sooner, and no long-term history of public counts.

claims.statement: Per search-index excerpts of the Developer Policies, when a user asks the API client to delete their stored data it must be deleted as soon as possible and within 7 calendar days, and when a user revokes consent through the client's own revocation mechanism the client must programmatically revoke the token right away and delete all Authorized Data obtained under that consent within 7 calendar days; the companion guide page is summarized as saying 30 days, which conflicts.
claims.design_implication: Build a disconnect-and-delete action that revokes the Google token immediately and purges that member's YouTube data within 7 days, using the stricter figure.

claims.statement: Per search-index excerpts, when a user revokes access through Google's security settings page rather than in the app, the client must detect this (for example by failing token refresh) and delete the associated data as soon as possible and within 30 calendar days of the revocation; one search summary gave 7 calendar days for this case, so the exact figure is unconfirmed.
claims.design_implication: Run a periodic token-validity check and purge data for any member whose token no longer refreshes, targeting 7 days to be safe under either reading.

claims.statement: A 2026 amendment (revision history entries dated May 4, 2026 and June 1, 2026) lets API clients that are audited, have an accepted Analytics & Reporting use case and applied through the quota extension form store statistical metrics such as views, likes, subscriber and comment counts for up to 36 calendar months, while titles, descriptions and comment text stay under the 30-day refresh-and-delete rule.
claims.design_implication: An unaudited small app does not get the 36-month allowance, so it must not keep historical YouTube statistics beyond 30 days unless it later passes an audit for that use case.

claims.statement: Authorized and Non-Authorized Data have different retention rules: certain Authorized Data types named in section III.E.4.b may be stored longer than 30 days provided the client re-verifies every 30 days that the user's authorization still stands (and that the video has not been deleted), all other Authorized Data is capped at 30 calendar days then delete or refresh, and Non-Authorized statistics have a flat 30-day cap with no longer-storage option.
claims.design_implication: Tag every stored YouTube value with whether it came from a member's OAuth consent or from public access, and apply the stricter rule when the tag is missing.

claims.statement: Developer Policies section III.A requires each API client to have users agree to a privacy policy before they can access its features, and that policy must clearly and comprehensively explain what user information, including API Data relating to users, the client accesses, collects, stores and otherwise uses.
claims.design_implication: The sign-in gate needs an explicit privacy-policy acceptance step before any YouTube data is shown or connected, even for a three-member private app.

claims.statement: Per search-index excerpts, API clients must display a link to YouTube's Terms of Service (https://www.youtube.com/t/terms) and state in their own terms that users agree to be bound by them, and the privacy policy must notify users that the client uses YouTube API Services, link to the Google Privacy Policy, and explain that users can revoke access via the Google security settings page at https://security.google.com/settings/security/permissions; the Google Privacy Policy link requirement was confirmed by only one summary.
claims.design_implication: Add the three links (YouTube Terms, Google Privacy Policy, Google security settings) to the app's terms and privacy pages before enabling any YouTube connection.

claims.statement: By default the Developer Policies forbid API clients from replacing API Data with similar independently calculated data or using API Data to create new or derived data or metrics, with the excerpted example that a client may not calculate a score that factors in likes, total views or any other API Data.
claims.design_implication: The dashboard should show raw YouTube figures as returned and must not compute a member score, rank or 'verified activity' rating that is derived from YouTube metrics.

claims.statement: The Developer Policies and the compliance guide allow non-YouTube data to appear alongside YouTube API data only with a clear and prominent disclosure that it is not from YouTube, and the guide lists as not permitted a 'user engagement' metric that combines YouTube engagement with other platforms and showing YouTube data next to other platforms' data without clarifying the types and sources.
claims.design_implication: YouTube and TikTok (or manual) figures must sit in separately labelled sections with their source named, and must never be summed into one cross-platform total or score.

claims.statement: The 'Additional policies for derived metrics and data storage' page permits custom scores and leaderboards (examples excerpted include a 'Top YouTuber by View Growth' leaderboard) only for audited developers who selected the Analytics & Reporting use case and applied through the quota extension form, effective June 1, 2026, and requires those metrics to be distinguished from metrics sourced from API Data.
claims.design_implication: A leaderboard built on YouTube metrics is off limits for an unaudited app; any ranking shown must be based on the app's own non-YouTube data and labelled as such.

claims.statement: A compliance audit via the Audit and Quota Extension Form is required only to be granted more than the default quota (10,000 units per day, with separate default buckets of 100 search.list calls and 100 videos.insert calls since June 2026), but the Terms of Service separately let YouTube monitor and audit any API client at any time without further notice.
claims.design_implication: A three-member app can run on default quota with no audit application, but must be fully policy-compliant from day one and should avoid search.list-heavy designs given the 100-call bucket.

claims.statement: None of the Developer Policies, compliance guide or Terms of Service excerpts retrieved showed any exemption from the storage, deletion, disclosure or derived-metric rules for small, private, sign-in-gated or non-commercial API clients.
claims.design_implication: Do not assume the app's small size or private access relaxes any YouTube data-handling duty; design to the full policy.

(Search summary only; docs do not say whether sandbox may be used indefinitely as a real private deployment or which Display scopes it exposes.)

claims.statement: The Data Portability API is open to qualified applicants globally but currently covers data only for TikTok users in the EEA and UK, and requires a separate Data Portability application (defined use case, ability to identify EEA/UK users, privacy and security review with high-fidelity UX mockups, typically 3-4 weeks) in addition to Login Kit approval. (Search summary only.)
claims.design_implication: For members outside the EEA/UK this route is unavailable, and even inside those regions the approval burden makes it unrealistic for a three-member private dashboard.

claims.statement: The Data Portability Data Types page lists a 'Like List' (date, video landing page link) and 'Comments' (date, comment content, original post landing page link) under the Full Archive (portability.all.single / .ongoing), whereas the narrower Activity category covers searches, share history, status and watch history. (Search summary only; category mapping was read from a flattened snippet.)

claims.statement: Google's server-side checklist for a Sign in with Google ID token is: verify the signature with Google's public keys, check that aud equals one of the app's client IDs, check that iss equals accounts.google.com or https://accounts.google.com, and check that exp has not passed (an hd check is added only when restricting sign-in to a Workspace/Cloud organization).
claims.design_implication: Treat a sign-in as authenticated only after all four checks pass on the server; a token merely decoded in the browser attests nothing.

claims.statement: The sub claim is the stable user identifier: Google describes it as unique among all Google Accounts and never reused (up to 255 case-sensitive ASCII characters) and says to key accounts on sub rather than email, because an email value may not be unique to the account and can change over time.
claims.design_implication: Key each member record on sub; the strongest identity statement the app can honestly make is 'this Google Account (sub) signed in', not anything about the person's social accounts.

claims.statement: Google says email, email_verified and hd together show whether Google is authoritative for an address: an @gmail.com address is Google-authoritative, email_verified true with hd present indicates a Google Workspace account, and when the email is not @gmail.com and hd is absent Google is not authoritative (email_verified can be true even though ownership of the third-party mailbox may have since changed).
claims.design_implication: Do not present an email as 'verified' on the strength of email_verified alone for non-Gmail, non-Workspace addresses; gate membership on an allowlist of sub values captured at enrollment.

claims.statement: The ID token reaches the backend by one of two routes: a JavaScript callback (required for One Tap and for the popup-mode button; the page's own code must then forward the credential) or an HTTP POST to login_uri carrying the token in a field named credential (redirect mode; login_uri must exactly match an authorized redirect URI of the OAuth client). callback and login_uri cannot both be set, and an optional nonce configuration value is embedded in the ID token for replay protection.
claims.design_implication: Either route delivers the same JWT, so the server-side verification in C1 is the only trust boundary; generate a per-request nonce and compare it to the nonce claim to reject replayed tokens.

claims.statement: For the login_uri POST, the Google library sets a g_csrf_token cookie and sends the same value as a g_csrf_token body parameter; the server must reject the request if either is missing or the two do not match (double-submit-cookie pattern), and this check comes in addition to, not instead of, ID-token verification.
claims.design_implication: Enforce g_csrf_token on the login endpoint; if the JavaScript-callback route is used instead, Google supplies no CSRF token for the app's own token-forwarding request (inferred), so the app must add its own CSRF protection there.

claims.statement: The setup guide's Content-Security-Policy guidance is to allow https://accounts.google.com/gsi/ in connect-src and frame-src and https://accounts.google.com/gsi/client in script-src; its Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy guidance is that no change is needed when FedCM renders the popups, but when FedCM is not used the page must send same-origin-allow-popups (a strict same-origin policy breaks the sign-in popup).
claims.design_implication: A hardened dashboard must ship these exact CSP allowances and COOP same-origin-allow-popups, otherwise sign-in silently fails and members cannot be authenticated at all.

claims.statement: In the current JavaScript and HTML references use_fedcm_for_prompt / data-use_fedcm_for_prompt is marked deprecated and 'ignored if used' (the integrator can no longer opt One Tap in or out of FedCM), while use_fedcm_for_button is an optional flag defaulting to false (Chrome desktop M125+, Android M128+). The migration guide tells integrators to stop relying on One Tap display-moment and skipped-reason methods, drop custom One Tap positioning, add allow="identity-credentials-get" on cross-origin parent iframes and allow the FedCM origins in CSP. No GIS-specific mandatory date was found: the 'mandatory from August 2025' date located belongs to the legacy Google Sign-In platform library page.
claims.design_implication: Use the plain Sign in with Google button as the primary path and treat One Tap as optional, since One Tap display is now browser-controlled through FedCM and cannot be reliably detected or forced.

claims.statement: The Sign in with Google ID token is not a credential for Google APIs: Google Identity Services' authentication API returns only ID tokens used to sign in, while a separate authorization request returns the authorization code or access token needed for data access, and the two must be invoked at separate moments.
claims.design_implication: Signing in with Google proves nothing about a member's YouTube channel; channel ownership can only be labelled verified after a separate OAuth grant followed by an authorized API call.

claims.statement: For server-side YouTube access the YouTube guide uses the OAuth 2.0 authorization-code (web server) flow, recommending access_type=offline to obtain a refresh token, include_granted_scopes=true for incremental authorization, and a state value that the callback compares with the value stored in the user's session; channels.list with mine=true is the documented authorized call that returns the authenticated user's own channel, whose id property is the channel ID.
claims.design_implication: A 'verified YouTube channel' label is honest only when the channel ID came from an authorized channels.list mine=true response obtained in that member's own consent flow, never from a typed or pasted ID.

claims.statement: Google's redirect-URI validation rules require the HTTPS scheme except for localhost URIs (including localhost IP addresses), forbid raw IP hosts other than localhost, and forbid fragments, wildcards, userinfo, path traversal and open redirects; the redirect_uri sent must exactly match a registered URI including scheme, case and trailing slash or the request fails with redirect_uri_mismatch.
claims.design_implication: Register one exact HTTPS callback per deployed origin plus an http://localhost callback for development; preview deployments on changing hostnames cannot complete the YouTube link flow.

claims.statement: The YouTube Data API scopes documented are youtube, youtube.readonly, youtube.force-ssl, youtube.upload, youtube.channel-memberships.creator, youtubepartner and youtubepartner-channel-audit, with advice to request the narrowest one; the documentation pages located do not publish a per-scope sensitive-versus-restricted classification (they say sensitivity is indicated in the Google Cloud Console), although Google's sensitive-scope verification page uses 'deleting a YouTube video' as an example of sensitive-scope access.
claims.design_implication: Request only youtube.readonly and confirm its classification in the Cloud Console scope picker before designing around it; do not assume from documentation alone that it avoids verification.

claims.statement: An External app that requests sensitive scopes must pass Google's sensitive-scope verification before unrestricted production use; reported requirements include domains the developer owns, a home page, a privacy policy, a least-privilege scope justification and an unlisted YouTube demo video of the consent flow and scope usage (Google's estimate about 10 business days; restricted scopes add a security assessment). Until verified, the app shows the unverified-app screen and is capped at 100 users over the lifetime of the project, a cap that cannot be reset.
claims.design_implication: For three members, full verification is disproportionate; the YouTube link should stay optional so the dashboard works without it and never depends on a verified OAuth app.

claims.statement: With an External user type and publishing status Testing, only up to 100 listed test users can authorize, and their authorizations, including any refresh token, expire 7 days after consent; the sole exception is an app requesting nothing beyond name, email address and user profile (userinfo.email, userinfo.profile, openid), where users need not be listed, see no warning and authorizations do not expire. Google's OAuth 2.0 overview page lists the same 7-day refresh-token rule and exception.
claims.design_implication: Plain Sign in with Google is unaffected by Testing status, but a YouTube grant made in Testing goes stale after 7 days, so any YouTube-derived label needs a last-attested timestamp and must downgrade when the grant lapses.

claims.statement: Google's help pages state no time limit on remaining in Testing status and say an app in Testing does not need verification, so a tiny private app can stay in Testing indefinitely at the cost of re-consenting YouTube scopes every 7 days; the documented alternative is the personal-use exception, where an In-production unverified app used by fewer than 100 users personally known to the developer may continue with users clicking through the unverified-app warning.
claims.design_implication: Either mode is workable for three members, but both mean the YouTube attestation is periodic or warning-gated, so the UI should show 'verified as of <date>' instead of a permanent verified badge.

claims.statement: The Google API Services User Data Policy (reported last updated February 15, 2024) applies Limited Use requirements to data from sensitive and restricted scopes: use only to provide or improve user-facing features, no transfers except for narrow reasons (user-consented features, security, legal compliance, merger or acquisition), no use for advertising, and no human reading except with explicit user consent, for security, for legal compliance or on aggregated data; the rules also cover data aggregated, anonymized or derived from those scopes, and the app must publicly disclose its compliance.
claims.design_implication: A stored YouTube channel ID and anything derived from it may be shown only for the member-facing dashboard feature the member consented to, and the privacy notice must say so.

claims.statement: Concrete deletion deadlines for stored YouTube data come from the YouTube API Services Developer Policies, not from the base User Data Policy (whose summarized text showed no standalone deletion deadline): delete a user's Authorized Data within 7 calendar days when they revoke through the app, within 30 calendar days when access is revoked through Google's security settings, and delete or re-verify stored data when a user requests deletion or authorization can no longer be confirmed (30 days).
claims.design_implication: The app needs an unlink action that revokes the token and deletes the stored channel ID, plus a periodic job that removes the channel ID and its verified label once the grant can no longer be refreshed.

claims.statement: Google's ID-token signing keys are published as a JWK set at https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs (the jwks_uri of the OpenID Connect discovery document; a PEM form also exists), are rotated regularly and should be re-fetched according to the response's Cache-Control header; Google recommends its API client libraries over hand-written validation, which for Node.js is google-auth-library's OAuth2Client.verifyIdToken with an audience argument (it checks signature, aud, exp and iss), and describes the tokeninfo endpoint as suitable for debugging only.
claims.design_implication: Use google-auth-library on the server and never pin or hardcode keys; a hand-rolled verifier that caches keys past Cache-Control will start rejecting or mis-accepting tokens after rotation.

claims.statement: Two 2025 changes affect small OAuth projects: client secrets are viewable and downloadable only at creation (new clients from June 2025, extended to existing clients from November 2025), and under an OAuth 2.0 policy entry dated October 27, 2025 Google may delete OAuth clients unused for 6 months (no token exchanges or configuration edits), with an email warning 30 days beforehand and roughly 30 days of recoverability after deletion.
claims.design_implication: Store the client secret securely at creation and monitor the project owner's mailbox, because a deleted client breaks sign-in and invalidates every existing YouTube grant and any label that depends on it.
